title: A grant is principal × capability × effect, with an optional where clause; scope '*' and an omitted operation list widen it
content:
```ts
type Grant = {
  id: string;            // stable; SET_GRANT upserts, REMOVE_GRANT deletes
  description: string;   // intent, shows in the audit trail
  effect: "allow" | "deny";
  principal:
    | { anyone: true }          // any signer, including anonymous
    | { address: string }       // one wallet, compared case-insensitively
    | { group: string }         // a powerhouse/reactor-group document id
    | { match: Condition };     // relationship, e.g. subject.address == doc.global.rtoAddress
  capability:
    | { can: "read"; scope?: string }
    | { can: "execute"; scope?: string; operation?: string[] };
  where?: Condition;     // the grant applies only when this holds
};
```

`scope` accepts `"*"` for every scope, and an absent scope means the same. Omitting `operation` on an execute capability covers every action in the scope. A `where` clause reads `subject.*`, `doc.<scope>.*` and `action.input.*`, which is how a grant can depend on the values of the operation it gates — e.g. the spec's toll statement lets an RTO read only the statement whose `rtoAddress` is their own.

Conditions are a small language — `eq/ne/in/notIn/lt/lte/gt/gte/exists/and/or/not` over `{ attr }` and `{ lit }` operands — required to be deterministic, total (never throw on any state shape), pure and JSON-serializable. A path that does not resolve, or resolves to an object or array, yields undefined, and every comparison with undefined is false.

The `document-acl` demo installs the canonical three-grant shape: an administrator's `execute` on scope `auth`, the administrator's `execute` on `*`, and `{anyone}` `execute` narrowed to `["ADD_ENTRY"]` on `global`. The recipes and the reference both warn that the administration grant should name `auth`, not `*`, because an allow on execute now confers read.
